== APPRAISAL INSTRUCTIONS (GEMINI_HANDOFF_BRIEF §3 Task D; RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1-2; APPRAISAL_FORM.md; CODEBOOK.md §8) ==
1. ACCESSIBILITY GATE:
   - If `Retrieval status` is `not_accessible` (or the paper text below says `[FULL TEXT NOT ACCESSIBLE]`), you MUST set `paper_read = "not accessible"`, `study_design_identified = "cannot_tell (full text not accessible)"`, `chosen_tool = "cannot_tell"`, `why_tool_chosen = "full text not accessible"`, `overall_rating = "cannot_tell"`, `domain_ratings = []`, all 7 `cross_tool_domains` fields to `"cannot_tell"`, `overall_narrative_summary = "Full text not accessible; no risk-of-bias appraisal performed."`, `where_found_summary = "not accessible"`, and `evidence_quotes = []`. NEVER guess study design or bias ratings from citation/title!

2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: No information / Not assessable: Single-wave cross-sectional survey with no longitudinal follow-up; the paper reports n = 652 (331 WRUA members, 321 non-members) but provides no information on target sample size, household refusal/non-response rates, or item-level missing data in the regressions.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Serious risk: Cross-sectional comparison lacks pre-intervention baseline poverty or water-access data, conditions on potentially endogenous post-treatment covariates (e.g., improved crops, electricity, credit access, livestock/TLUs), and relies on questionable exclusion restrictions (MWS-River, MWS-Borehole, Water conflict) that are plausibly affected by CWDP/WRUA water provision and violate exclusion for water poverty (Water conflict enters the WPI directly in Table A2 and has Coef. = 0.80, SE = 0.18 in Table A1 Model 5; joint falsification tests were not re-estimated after dropping MWS-Piped water).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak / Moderate concern: The study situates Water Resource Users Associations (WRUAs) within Kenya's Water Act 2002 and Water Act 2016, but operationalizes the legal/institutional exposure solely as a cross-sectional household binary indicator (WRUA member = 1 vs. 0) that conflates Community Water Development Project (CWDP) water-supply group membership with sub-catchment WRUA regulatory governance and omits membership duration, water-permit status, fee payment, and rule enforcement.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Serious risk: Exposure and outcomes were collected contemporaneously through unblinded face-to-face CAPI interviews; subjective poverty and water-perception items are susceptible to self-report bias, and the Water Poverty Index embeds both right-hand-side socioeconomic covariates (land ownership, title, formal education, non-farm occupation, credit access) and the selection instrument (Water conflict) directly inside the composite outcome index.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak / Serious concern: All four poverty outcomes (annual consumption, annual income, Economic Ladder Question, and polychoric-PCA Water Poverty Index) rely on single-visit household self-reports without physical water-quality or meter verification; Equation (A1) omits the Resources component in text while Table A2 lists five components; socioeconomic confounders and the Water conflict instrument are built into the WPI; and water poverty is defined via an arbitrary sample-relative 40th percentile cut-off.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Serious risk: No pre-registration or pre-analysis plan exists; continuous outcomes analyzed in a 2020 companion paper on the same catchment are dichotomized here (including a sample-relative 40th percentile cut-off for water poverty); Table 7 reports a positive IPW ATT for subjective poverty (+0.091**, SE = 0.039) whereas the text claims a 9% reduction; and Table A1 omits significance stars on Water conflict (Coef. = 0.80, SE = 0.18, z = 4.44) in the water-poverty falsification model while claiming validity.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Serious risk: Cross-sectional prevalent-user design recruiting existing WRUA members (n = 331) and non-members (n = 321) in September–December 2019 long after intervention uptake, using disproportionate stratified sampling across eight sub-catchments of unknown population size without reported sampling weights, and drawing simple random samples from a WRUA list with unreported non-response rates.

domain_ratings.justification: Rated Serious. The study compares prevalent WRUA members (n = 331) and non-members (n = 321) using a single cross-sectional survey without pre-membership baseline measures of poverty, wealth, or water access. Both the ESP equations (Tables 5–6) and the PSM/IPW specifications condition on contemporaneous covariates plausibly affected by WRUA/CWDP participation (e.g., growing improved crops, electricity connection, credit access, extension, livestock/TLUs). Furthermore, the ESP exclusion restrictions (MWS-River, MWS-Borehole, and Water conflict) are weak/invalid: CWDPs/WRUAs directly supply piped compound water (82.8% of members vs. 21.5% of non-members), making river/borehole reliance a consequence of non-membership; Water conflict is included directly as a sub-indicator of the Uses component of the Water Poverty Index (Table A2), violating exclusion by construction; in Table A1 Model 5 (water poverty for non-members), Water conflict has Coef. = 0.80 with SE = 0.18 (z = 4.44, p < 0.001, unstarred in the table); and after dropping MWS-Piped water for failing falsification, the authors did not report a re-estimated falsification test for the remaining three instruments.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domain_ratings.justification: Rated Serious. Participants were sampled cross-sectionally between September and December 2019 as prevalent WRUA members and non-members rather than at the start of membership/intervention, introducing prevalent-user survival/selection bias. In addition, eight sub-catchments were sampled disproportionately because household population sizes were unknown (with no sampling weights reported in estimation), and simple random sampling of households was conducted 'using a list from the WRUAs', raising substantial concern about how non-member households appeared on WRUA lists and whether sampled non-members represent the broader non-member smallholder population. Household refusal/non-response rates are not reported.

Rated Moderate. WRUA membership is recorded as a binary indicator (Wi = 1 for 331 members, Wi = 0 for 321 non-members), informed by WRUA lists and household survey interviews. However, the paper notes that smallholders join Community Water Development Projects (CWDPs) which obtain group WRUA membership (Section 1), and the binary indicator conflates CWDP piped-water group membership with sub-catchment WRUA governance while omitting membership duration, timing of entry relative to poverty status, and intensity of participation. Because classification was recorded contemporaneously with outcomes, historical misclassification of exposure timing cannot be ruled out.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domain_ratings.justification: Rated No information. The paper provides no information on household adherence to WRUA water-abstraction or catchment-conservation rules, fee/tariff compliance, switching between membership and non-membership over time, external donor/NGO co-interventions targeting specific CWDPs, or sub-catchment governance spillovers from WRUAs to non-member households residing within the same eight WRUA sub-catchments.

Rated No information. Tables 2 and 3 report 331 WRUA members and 321 non-members (total N = 652), matching the stated sample size in Section 2.1, but the paper provides no information on initial target sample size, survey non-response/refusal rates, item-level missingness across income, consumption, or the 22 WPI items, or exact estimation sample sizes in Tables 5, 6, 7, and A1.

Rated Serious. All four binary poverty outcomes were derived from unblinded face-to-face CAPI interviews conducted simultaneously with exposure ascertainment. Subjective poverty (Economic Ladder Question) and multiple WPI perceptions (water sufficiency, water quality, taste, smell) are directly susceptible to respondent perception bias linked to CWDP/WRUA participation, while annual income and consumption rely on unverified recall without stated recall windows. Crucially, the Water Poverty Index suffers from mechanical construction flaws: Equation (A1) text omits the Resources component while Table A2 includes five components; Table A2 embeds right-hand-side socioeconomic covariates (land ownership, land title, formal education, non-farming occupation, credit access) inside the WPI Capacity component and embeds the selection instrument (Water conflict) inside the WPI Uses component; and water poverty is dichotomized at a sample-relative 40th percentile threshold.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 6–7, 10–11, 22 (Sections 2.1, 2.2, 3.1; Table 1, Table 3, Table A2)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of the reported result
domain_ratings.justification: Rated Serious (no pre-analysis plan or study protocol is reported, and multiple concrete internal reporting inconsistencies are present). Continuous welfare outcomes analyzed in a companion paper on the same catchment (Mwaura et al., 2020) are dichotomized here alongside an arbitrary 40th-percentile cut-off for water poverty. In Table 7, the Inverse Probability Weighting ATT for subjective poverty is reported as +0.091** (SE = 0.039), indicating higher poverty, whereas the text states that IPW reduced subjective poverty by about 9%. In Table A1 Model 5, the falsification coefficient on Water conflict for non-member water poverty is 0.80 (SE = 0.18, z = 4.44, p < 0.001), yet significance stars are omitted and the text claims Water conflict passed the falsification test without re-running the joint test after dropping MWS-Piped water.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Mwaura et al. (2021) evaluate the impact of household membership in Water Resource Users Associations (WRUAs) / Community Water Development Projects (CWDPs) on four binary poverty outcomes (consumption poverty, income poverty, subjective Economic Ladder poverty, and polychoric-PCA water poverty) using a 2019 cross-sectional survey of 652 rural smallholder households (331 WRUA members and 321 non-members) in Kenya's Upper Ewaso Ng'iro North Catchment Area. Because the study estimates causal treatment effects (ATT and ATU) of an institutional water-governance intervention against a non-member comparator using Full Information Maximum Likelihood Endogenous Switching Probit (ESP) with exclusion restrictions alongside Propensity Score Matching (PSM) and Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW), ROBINS-I is the appropriate appraisal instrument. Overall risk of bias is rated Serious, driven by Serious concerns in confounding (D1), participant selection (D2), outcome measurement (D6), and selective/inconsistent result reporting (D7), Moderate concern in intervention classification (D3), and No information on intervention deviations/spillovers (D4) and missing data (D5). Key threats include prevalent-user cross-sectional sampling drawn from WRUA lists without baseline pre-treatment data or sampling weights; conditioning on post-treatment covariates; invalid exclusion restrictions (notably 'Water conflict', which is mechanically embedded inside the Water Poverty Index in Table A2 and exhibits an unstarred z = 4.44 association with non-member water poverty in Table A1 Model 5); mechanical contamination of the Water Poverty Index with right-hand-side socioeconomic covariates; and reporting discrepancies such as a positive IPW ATT (+0.091**) for subjective poverty in Table 7 narrated in the text as a 9% poverty reduction.
raw_response.study_design_identified: Cross-sectional comparative household survey (n = 652; 331 WRUA members vs. 321 non-members) applying quasi-experimental / econometric treatment-effect estimators (FIML Endogenous Switching Probit with instrumental-variable exclusion restrictions, Propensity Score Matching, and Inverse Probability Weighting)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Study design, sampling, variable construction, and econometric identification were appraised from Section 1 (PDF pp. 3–5), Section 2.1–2.4 (PDF pp. 5–9), Section 3.1–3.3 (PDF pp. 9–17), Tables 1–7 (PDF pp. 7, 10–14, 17), and Appendix Tables A1–A2 (PDF p. 22).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: Although data come from a single 2019 cross-sectional survey, the study explicitly frames WRUA membership (institutionalized under Kenya's Water Act 2002 and Water Act 2016) as a binary policy/institutional intervention evaluated against a non-member comparator group (n = 331 vs. n = 321) to estimate causal Average Treatment Effects on the Treated (ATT) and Untreated (ATU) via Endogenous Switching Probit (with IV exclusion restrictions), Propensity Score Matching (PSM), and Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW). Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, non-randomized intervention/policy evaluations using IV/PSM/IPW comparator designs are appraised with ROBINS-I rather than the JBI analytical cross-sectional checklist.
